title: What is a default?
subtitle: When a borrower fails to pay debt on time
openingQuestion: A company misses a bond interest payment by just one day. Does that count as a default?
openingOptions: Only government bonds have a default concept
No, default only applies at bankruptcy
No, it has to be at least a year late to count as default
Yes - any breach of a debt obligation, even a short delay, can trigger a technical default
explanation: A default is when an issuer fails to meet a debt obligation exactly as agreed: a late coupon, a late principal payment, or a breached covenant. A 'technical default' happens even from a plain contract breach, well before bankruptcy is on the table. Rating agencies cut a credit rating as soon as any sign of default shows up.

diagram.label: A loan contract carries obligations to repay principal, pay interest, and honor covenants
Breaching any one of them is a default
Breaching a covenant without missing a payment: technical default
Lenders gain the right to demand immediate repayment of the entire loan

realWorldExample.description: Evergrande defaulted on its USD bonds in 2021 when it failed to pay interest to international bondholders on time, even though the company kept operating - a clear illustration that default does not mean immediate bankruptcy.

quiz.question: What does the recovery rate mean in a default?
options: How fast a company restores its profit after restructuring debt
The percentage of original principal a bondholder recovers after liquidation
The share of companies in an industry that exit default status each year
The new rate applied to the debt after renegotiating with creditors
quiz.explanation: Recovery rate = the amount a bondholder actually receives / original face value. Secured bonds usually have a higher recovery rate (60-80%) than unsecured bonds (20-40%).

quiz.question: Why can a "technical default" (a contract breach, not necessarily a full loss of ability to pay) still cause severe consequences for a company, even while it can still pay part of its obligations?
options: It legally forces the company to file for bankruptcy
It causes every outstanding bond to be delisted immediately
It triggers cross-default clauses in the company's other loan agreements
It only lowers the credit rating without changing the current debt obligation
quiz.explanation: Cross-default clauses, common in loan agreements, are why a small technical breach can escalate into a full-blown crisis - other creditors gain the right to treat their own loans as breached too, triggering simultaneous demands for immediate repayment.

quiz.question: A bond has a face value of 1 billion VND and a recovery rate of 40%. How much does the bondholder get back?
options: 40 million (= 1 billion × 4%, a decimal-place slip)
600 million (= 1 billion × 60%, taking the lost portion instead)
1.4 billion (= 1 billion × 1.4, adding the 40% instead of applying it)
400 million (= 1 billion × 40% recovered)
quiz.explanation: Recovery rate is the portion recovered, not the portion lost. Secured bonds typically recover 60-80%, while unsecured bonds can recover as little as 20-30%.

quiz.question: How does default differ from bankruptcy?
options: Default is a breach of obligation; bankruptcy is a legal proceeding
Default applies to companies, bankruptcy to individuals
Default happens only after a court declares insolvency
The two terms are identical, just industry-specific labels
quiz.explanation: Missing a single interest payment already counts as default, even while the company keeps operating normally and can catch up later. Bankruptcy is a much further step, and most defaults never get there.

quiz.question: Why do secured bonds usually have a higher recovery rate?
options: Because the law requires this group to be paid first
Because bondholders can seize and sell that specific collateral ahead of other creditors
Because only highly rated companies issue this type of bond
Because the collateral is always worth many times the loan
quiz.explanation: Collateral creates a separate line: this group has a claim on a specific asset instead of sharing the residual pool with everyone else. The 60-80% versus 20-30% gap is exactly the value of that position.

keyTakeaways: Default: a breach of debt obligation, not necessarily bankruptcy
A technical default can happen from a covenant breach alone
Recovery rate depends on whether the bond is backed by collateral

practicePrompt.question: A company misses a bond interest payment on time because of a temporary cash-flow crunch, but keeps operating normally and pays the missed amount later. Is this bankruptcy, and what is the precise term for this situation?
options: This is bankruptcy, since the company failed to meet its debt obligation
Not bankruptcy - default is a breach of debt obligation that can be remedied
This is called a technical default and it always leads to bankruptcy within a few months
There is no technical term for this situation - it is simply a late payment
practicePrompt.explanation: Default: a breach of debt obligation, not necessarily bankruptcy. Default comes in degrees - from a mild covenant breach (technical default) to a total loss of ability to pay that leads to bankruptcy - two related but distinct concepts.

summary.keyIdea: Default: a breach of debt obligation, not necessarily bankruptcy
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: A technical default can happen from a covenant breach alone

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Look up news of a recent default or technical default (domestic or international) and identify whether the cause was a late coupon, late principal, or a covenant breach.
application.secondary: Telling these forms of default apart helps you read financial news more accurately.

sections.text: A default is when a bond issuer fails to meet an obligation it agreed to - a late interest payment, a late return of principal, or even simply a breach of a clause in the loan agreement. The key thing to understand: default does not mean immediate bankruptcy, and it does not always mean the company has completely lost its ability to pay.
Technical default: a breach without a loss of ability to pay

A 'technical default' happens when a company breaches a covenant in a loan agreement - for example, its debt-to-equity ratio crosses an allowed threshold - even while the company is still paying interest and principal in full and on time. Technically, this still counts as a default event, and credit rating agencies typically cut the rating as soon as this sign appears, even though the company has not actually lost its ability to pay.
Cross-default: when a small breach spreads into a crisis

What makes a technical default dangerous is the cross-default clause common in loan agreements: when a company breaches one loan, its other loans - even ones with no direct connection - can automatically be treated as breached too. Other creditors then gain the right to demand immediate repayment, turning one seemingly small initial breach into a widespread liquidity crisis. Evergrande (China) in 2021 is a textbook example: the company defaulted on international USD bonds by failing to pay interest to bondholders on time, even as it kept running its business - a clear illustration that default and bankruptcy are two different concepts.

items: Default: a breach of a debt obligation - late interest, late principal, or a covenant breach - not necessarily bankruptcy
Technical default: a breach of a contract term even while still paying debt in full
Cross-default: one breach can trigger a chain reaction of breaches across other loans
Recovery rate = the amount a bondholder actually receives / original face value after asset liquidation
